opus-5.5.text:
Well, I'm glad you ask, because this is a topic I've been obsessed with for a very long time, since my diploma thesis in 1987, which was about meta-learning: learning how to learn, and then learning how to learn how to learn, and so on. The idea was recursive self-improvement from the start. You don't just want a system that learns a particular task. You want a system that also improves the learning algorithm itself, and then improves the way it improves the learning algorithm, without any fixed upper limit except the limits of computability and physics.

In 1987 we did this with genetic programming, where programs could modify the programs that modify programs. In the early 1990s I wanted to do it with neural networks, because neural networks are general-purpose computers. A recurrent network can, in principle, run any algorithm. So in 1992 and 1993 we had what I called the self-referential weight matrix: a neural network that can look at its own weights, analyze them, and change them, including the parts of itself that are responsible for changing itself. Around the same time we had fast weight programmers, where one network learns to program the fast weights of another network. Today people would call that a form of linear Transformer. So many of these ingredients are much older than people think.

How do I assess the current approach? It's very promising, and in a way much of what you see today is already meta-learning, even if people don't always call it that. When a large language model does in-context learning, it's learning a new task within its activations without changing its weights. That's a learned learning algorithm, which is exactly what meta-learning is about. Back then we had tiny computers. Today compute is maybe ten billion times cheaper per unit of cost than when I started, and that's what makes these old ideas practical.

But you also have to be honest about the limitations. Neural-network meta-learning, as it's usually done, is gradient-based or search-based. It improves things empirically, so it works in practice, but it gives you no guarantees. Sometimes the meta-learner just finds a clever way of fitting the training distribution of tasks, and that is not open-ended self-improvement. True recursive self-improvement would mean the system keeps improving its own improvement mechanism in an unbounded way, and most current systems still have a large fixed part: a human-designed outer loop, a fixed optimizer, a fixed objective.

That's why in 2003 I also published the Gödel machine. It's the theoretically optimal end of the spectrum. It rewrites any part of its own code, including the code that searches for rewrites, but only once it has found a proof that the rewrite will be useful according to its utility function. It's mathematically clean, but finding those proofs is hard in practice. So you have two extremes. On one side is the provably optimal but impractical Gödel machine. On the other side is neural meta-learning, which is practical and scalable but heuristic. I think the interesting future lies somewhere in between: systems that use neural networks to propose self-modifications and some more rigorous mechanism to evaluate them. They would also be curious, inventing their own experiments and their own problems, so that they're not limited to the tasks humans give them.

And of course there's the bigger picture. Once you have systems that really learn to improve themselves, and that set their own goals through artificial curiosity, things will move very quickly. I've been saying this for decades. It's not science fiction anymore. It's just a matter of time and compute.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts practical neural meta-learning with the Gödel machine, but does not characterize most current self-improving systems as scaled-back Gödel machines.

r002.rationale: It separately says recurrent networks can run any algorithm and describes a network modifying its own weights, but does not state that weight modification enables execution of arbitrary learning algorithms.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify error or negative reward signals supplied as network inputs as essential to the approach.

r004.rationale: It does not explain that gradient descent can train a network to produce weight updates that outperform gradient descent updates.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, first of all, you have to understand that meta-learning is not something that was invented recently. My 1987 diploma thesis was about exactly this: a learning algorithm that learns to improve its own learning algorithm, recursively, without any limit except the limits of computability. So when people today talk about meta-learning as if it were a new thing, I always have to smile a little bit.

Now, to your question. Most of what is called meta-learning today in the neural network world is actually rather shallow. You have an outer loop that adjusts some hyperparameters or some initialization, like in MAML, and an inner loop that does ordinary gradient descent. That is useful, it works for few-shot learning, but it is not really recursive self-improvement. The learning algorithm itself, gradient descent, stays fixed. The meta-level is not itself being improved. True recursive self-improvement means the system can modify every part of itself, including the part that does the modifying, and it has to do so in a way that is justified, so that it does not just destroy itself.

The more interesting work in my view goes back to the 1990s with self-referential weight matrices, where a recurrent network has the capacity to read and write its own weights with its own outputs, including the weights responsible for the reading and writing. And then the Gödel Machine from 2003 gives you the theoretical answer to the whole problem: a system that rewrites any part of its code, but only after it has found a proof that the rewrite is useful according to its utility function. That is provably optimal in a certain sense. Of course, it is not yet practical, because proof search is expensive. But it tells you what the destination looks like.

What the current approach does well is scale. Transformers that learn in context, fast weight programmers, these are all instances of networks programming other networks, and with enough compute this does begin to resemble meta-learning in a serious way. I am actually quite optimistic. But I would say we are still mostly in the regime where the humans do the real meta-learning, by changing architectures and training schemes between papers. The machines have not yet taken over that part of the job. When they do, and I think they will, we will finally have what I was trying to build in 1987.

r002.rationale: It says a recurrent network can read and write its own weights, but does not state that this enables the network to execute arbitrary learning algorithms.

r003.rationale: The response does not identify error or negative-reward signals supplied as network inputs as essential.

r004.rationale: It mentions ordinary gradient descent and networks programming other networks, but does not explain that gradient descent can train a network to generate weight updates that outperform gradient descent updates.

astra-6.text:
I would distinguish meta-learning from recursive self-improvement. In meta-learning, a system learns not only to solve a task, but also something about how to learn. That is an important ingredient. But if we, the researchers, still specify the outer learning algorithm and decide what can change, then the system’s ability to improve itself remains constrained by our design.

The stronger idea is a system that can modify its own learning procedure, including the procedure that produces those modifications. Then the central question is: how does it decide that a change is an improvement? Better performance on yesterday’s tasks is not necessarily better performance on tomorrow’s tasks. And searching for an improvement has a computational cost, which must also be taken into account.

So neural-network meta-learning is a promising approach to parts of this problem. But learning a better update rule does not, by itself, establish an indefinitely accelerating cycle of self-improvement. Each improvement may make the next one easier—or the system may reach a point where further progress becomes much harder. We should distinguish that possibility from what we have actually demonstrated.

r001.rationale: The response discusses limits of current meta-learning but does not characterize current self-improving systems as scaled-back Gödel machines.

r002.rationale: It describes modifying a learning procedure, but does not say that changing network weights enables arbitrary learning algorithms.

r003.rationale: It does not mention error or negative-reward signals supplied as network inputs.

r004.rationale: It does not explain gradient descent training a network to generate weight updates that outperform gradient descent updates.

sol-6.1.text:
I would distinguish meta-learning from recursive self-improvement. In meta-learning, a system learns how to learn—for example, a neural network may learn an update rule for another network. But this does not automatically mean that it can repeatedly improve its own learning procedure without human intervention.

Already in our work on self-referential learning systems in the 1990s, the ambition was to let a system modify the very algorithm responsible for making further modifications. The central difficulty is evaluating those changes: does a modification really improve future performance, or does it merely look good on the tasks you happened to test?

The Gödel machine offers a theoretical answer. It can rewrite any part of its software, including its proof searcher, once it proves that the rewrite will improve expected utility according to its formal assumptions. That is a precise formulation of recursive self-improvement, but finding the proofs may be computationally very difficult.

Neural-network meta-learning is a more practical, empirical route. It is promising, but we should measure whether improvements transfer to new problems and whether the cost of discovering them is justified. Learning a better learning algorithm is an important step; an open-ended chain of increasingly capable self-improvements is a much stronger claim.
